title: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
summary: Why people route around security, warnings and MFA that work, pretexts, deepfakes and help-desk takeovers, SIM swaps and insiders, locks, badges and tailgating, and testing people ethically.
outcomes: Explain with usable-security research why people bypass costly controls, and redesign a control so the safe path is the default
Break a pretext into stages and name the process rule that defeats each, without relying on spotting lies
Design a help-desk verification policy that rejects researchable facts and needs out-of-band proof for privileged accounts
Explain how SIM swaps, bribed insiders and deepfake calls bypass people, and which controls remove their value
Lay out physical zones, explain what locks, master keys and badges prove, and detect tailgating and cloning in access logs
Write rules of engagement and metrics for authorised social engineering and physical tests that measure processes, not people
Respond to a reported social engineering success and build a reporting culture that keeps reports coming

lessons.title: Security is a secondary task: why people work around it

blocks.md:
Picture an office where the IT policy forces a new password every month. A clerk who must remember six of them writes them on a sticky note under the keyboard. The policy was meant to make guessing harder; in practice it put every password on paper. The phishing course showed that attackers pick people because people can be talked into things. This course starts from the other side: people also *work around* security that costs them too much, and that gap is something defenders build, not something users choose out of carelessness.

The study of this is called **usable security** (designing security mechanisms that the people expected to use them can actually use correctly) or, more broadly, **human factors** in security. CyBOK (the Cyber Security Body of Knowledge, a structured map of the field) gives Human Factors its own knowledge area, next to the technical ones.

**Case: "Users are not the enemy" (1999).** Anne Adams and Martina Angela Sasse, usable-security researchers, surveyed 139 people with a web questionnaire and then interviewed 30 employees in two organisations about passwords. Half (50%) of questionnaire respondents wrote their passwords down in one form or another. One employee explained the link directly: "because I was forced into changing it every month I had to write it down." Another 50% built related passwords (name1, name2, name3) to cope, which made them easier to guess and harder to recall.

Their diagnosis was about communication, not stupidity. Security departments typecast users as "inherently insecure", at worst "the enemy within", and told them as little as possible. Users, in turn, saw many mechanisms as obstacles to their work. The paper's conclusion: "Users have to be treated as partners".

**The economics: Herley's "So long, and no thanks for the externalities" (2009).** Cormac Herley, a researcher at Microsoft Research, argued that users' rejection of security advice is "entirely rational from an economic perspective". Advice shields people from the *direct* cost of an attack, which hits only the few who become victims, but charges *everyone* an indirect cost in effort every day. An **externality** is a cost that falls on someone other than the party who causes it; Herley's point is that security advice externalises its cost onto users' time.

Herley's worked example uses round numbers: about 180 million online adults in the US, user time valued at twice the US minimum wage (2 x USD 7.25 per hour), and Herley's own earlier estimate of USD 60 million a year in US phishing losses. The script below redoes the arithmetic.

blocks.code:
adults = 180e6          # US online adults (Herley, 2009)
wage = 2 * 7.25         # twice the US minimum wage, USD per hour
losses = 60e6           # Herley's estimate of US annual phishing losses, USD

hour = adults * wage
minute_a_day = hour / 60 * 365
print(f"one hour of everyone's time:  USD {hour/1e9:.2f} billion")
print(f"one minute a day for a year:  USD {minute_a_day/1e9:.1f} billion")
print(f"ratio to phishing losses:     {minute_a_day/losses:.0f}x")
print(f"most a user could save/year:  USD {losses/adults:.2f}")
print(f"break-even at minimum wage:   {losses/adults/7.25*60:.1f} minutes")

# Output:
# one hour of everyone's time:  USD 2.61 billion
# one minute a day for a year:  USD 15.9 billion
# ratio to phishing losses:     265x
# most a user could save/year:  USD 0.33
# break-even at minimum wage:   2.8 minutes
blocks.caption: Herley's 2009 arithmetic, recomputed. The inputs are the paper's assumptions, not current measurements.

blocks.title: Yearly cost of a daily security chore versus the loss it prevents

x.label: minutes per day of user effort

scenes.caption: The rising line is the cost of asking every US online adult to spend x minutes a day on one security task, valued at twice the minimum wage. The flat line is Herley's estimate of all US phishing losses: USD 0.06 billion a year.
At one minute a day the chore costs about USD 15.9 billion a year, roughly 265 times the losses it could at best prevent. This is the 'two orders of magnitude' in Herley's abstract.
Value time at the bare minimum wage (USD 7.25) and the gap barely moves: still over 100 times. The conclusion does not hinge on the exact wage; it comes from charging everyone to protect a few.

blocks.md: Misconception: "people ignore security because they do not care". Adams and Sasse found people inventing their own schemes to comply, and Herley shows that ignoring costly advice is often the rational choice. When most people bypass a control, treat it as a design defect in the control.

**Why this matters for social engineering.** Attackers live in the gap between the official process and what people actually do. A help desk measured on how fast it closes tickets, a finance team buried in payment approvals, a receptionist told to be welcoming: each is a place where the secure path costs more than the quick one. The rest of this course follows that thread through warnings, passwords, phone calls, help desks, badges and doors.

**Defender view.** Before adding a rule, estimate who pays for it and how often; prefer controls that work without user effort (blocking, secure defaults); and ask the people who do the work where security slows them down, because that is where they will route around it.

Every security control spends someone's time and attention. Spend it where it buys the most risk reduction, automate the rest, and treat widespread workarounds as evidence that the control is badly designed.

blocks.question: A company forces monthly password changes. An audit finds many passwords on sticky notes. What does Adams and Sasse's study suggest is the main cause?
options: Employees are careless and need stricter penalties
Sticky notes are too easy to buy
The policy demands more memorisation than people can manage, so they write passwords down to cope
Monthly changes are too infrequent
blocks.explain: Their respondents linked writing passwords down directly to forced changes and to having many passwords. Penalties do not reduce the memory load; changing the policy does.

blocks.question: Herley argues that ignoring a piece of security advice can be rational. Which condition makes that most likely?
options: The advice costs every user effort every day, while the harm it prevents falls on a small fraction of users
The advice comes from a government agency
The advice protects against a very common attack
The advice is free to follow
blocks.explain: A daily cost multiplied across everyone easily exceeds a rare loss to a few. Advice that is cheap, or that prevents frequent and costly harm, does not fit Herley's argument.

lessons.title: Why Johnny can't encrypt: usability is a security property

blocks.md:
In 1999 email encryption existed and was free. Few people used it. Was that because the software looked ugly? Alma Whitten (Carnegie Mellon University) and J. D. Tygar (University of California, Berkeley) tested a program that had a good interface by ordinary standards, and found that ordinary standards were the problem. Their paper, "Why Johnny Can't Encrypt" (USENIX Security Symposium, 1999), started usable security as a research field.

The program was **PGP 5.0** (Pretty Good Privacy, an email encryption tool). PGP uses **public-key cryptography**: each person has a key pair, a public key that others use to encrypt messages to them and a private key that only they hold to decrypt. To send Ana a secret, you must encrypt it with *Ana's* public key, which you first have to obtain.

**The test.** Twelve participants, all experienced email users with some college education, none able to explain public versus private keys beforehand, got 90 minutes to send a signed and encrypted secret to their "campaign team". Results:

- Only one third (4 of 12) correctly signed and encrypted a message in 90 minutes.
- One quarter (3 of 12) emailed the secret **without encryption** by accident; one of them believed encryption had happened automatically.
- One could not work out how to encrypt at all.
- Of the eleven who could encrypt, seven encrypted to the team using **their own** public key, so the team could not read it.
- One generated key pairs for each team member instead of getting theirs.

Several worried that clicking their key-pair icon would publish their private key.

blocks.title: Whitten and Tygar (1999): 12 participants, 90 minutes, PGP 5.0

scenes.caption: Out of twelve experienced email users, only four managed the whole task: sign, encrypt to the right keys, send. That is the one third in the paper's conclusion.
Seven encrypted with their own public key. The software worked; the person's mental model of the keys did not, and nothing on screen told them.
Three sent the secret in plaintext while exploring. That is the barn door property: no later fix can un-send it.
One never found how to encrypt at all. The categories overlap (a person can appear in two), so they do not sum to twelve.

blocks.md:
**What engineers took from it.** The errors were not random. They came from a mismatch between the user's mental model ("a key locks things, so I lock it with my key") and the system's model. An interface that is pleasant but lets people make silent, irreversible mistakes fails the definition above at points 2 and 3.

Design rules that follow:

- **Make the secure path the default path**, so forgetting a step fails safe.
- **Fail loudly and before the damage**, not after (barn door).
- **Remove decisions** people cannot make well, such as choosing which key to trust, when software can make them.

blocks.code:
KEYS = {"ana@corp.example": "ana-public-key"}   # recipients we hold keys for

# Unsafe design: encryption is an option the user must remember to turn on.
def send_v1(to, body, encrypt=False):
    return f"to {to}: {'ENCRYPTED' if encrypt else 'PLAINTEXT'} {body!r}"

# Safer design: the secure path is the only path, and failure is loud.
def send_v2(to, body):
    key = KEYS.get(to)
    if key is None:
        raise ValueError(f"no public key for {to}; message NOT sent")
    return f"to {to}: ENCRYPTED with {key}"

print(send_v1("ana@corp.example", "the secret"))   # forgot the flag
print(send_v2("ana@corp.example", "the secret"))
try:
    send_v2("bo@corp.example", "the secret")
except ValueError as e:
    print("error:", e)

# Output:
# to ana@corp.example: PLAINTEXT 'the secret'
# to ana@corp.example: ENCRYPTED with ana-public-key
# error: no public key for bo@corp.example; message NOT sent
blocks.caption: Two API designs for the same feature. In v1 forgetting a flag silently sends plaintext; in v2 the only way to send is encrypted, and a missing key stops the send.

blocks.md: The same pattern shows up far from email. Any process where the safe action needs an extra step (an optional MFA check, a 'please verify' line in a help-desk script, a door that must be pulled shut) will be skipped under pressure. Make the safe outcome what happens when nobody does anything special.

blocks.question: In the study, seven participants encrypted messages to their team with their own public key. What kind of failure was this?
options: A bug in PGP's encryption code
Participants were not motivated to finish the task
The team members' email software was misconfigured
A mismatch between the user's mental model of keys and how public-key encryption works, with no feedback showing the error
blocks.explain: PGP encrypted exactly as asked. The users misunderstood whose key to use, and the interface gave no warning until the team replied that they could not read the message.

blocks.question: Which of Whitten and Tygar's properties explains why one accidental plaintext email is so serious?
options: The abstraction property
The barn door property
The unmotivated user property
The lack of feedback property
blocks.explain: Once the secret has been sent unprotected, nobody can be sure it was not read. Prevention has to happen before the mistake, because no fix after it restores secrecy.

lessons.title: Warnings people heed: browser warnings and opinionated design

blocks.md:
A browser is about to load a page whose TLS certificate does not check out. TLS (Transport Layer Security, the protocol behind HTTPS; its older versions were called SSL, Secure Sockets Layer, which is why research papers say "SSL warnings") is supposed to prove you reached the real site. Most of the time the cause is harmless, such as an expired certificate on a small site. Occasionally it is an attacker in the middle. The browser cannot tell which, so it asks the user, who usually knows even less.

How often do people **click through** (proceed despite) such warnings, and can design change that?

blocks.title: Clickthrough rates in the field, May and June 2013

scenes.caption: Malware and phishing warnings: most users stopped. Low clickthrough is the goal, because these warnings rarely fire on safe sites.
SSL warnings: a third of Firefox users and 70.2% of Chrome users went on. Different users, but the same kind of risk; the authors conclude a warning's user experience can strongly change behaviour.

blocks.md:
**Redesigning the warning (2015).** Felt and colleagues at Google tried to build an SSL warning that people would both *understand* and *follow* (adherence: choosing the safe option). They reported honestly that they "ultimately failed at our goal of a well-understood warning". Adherence, however, rose by nearly 30 percentage points, which they attributed to **opinionated design**: "the use of visual design cues to promote a recommended course of action". The safe choice became a bright blue button; the unsafe one became a dark grey text link hidden behind an "Advanced" link. After release as the Chrome 37 warning, adherence in the field rose from 37% to 62%.

The paper also notes that such hurdles (extra clicks to proceed) improve adherence by 2 to 15% depending on their complexity.

blocks.prompt: A warning fires on every expired certificate, including on internal test sites everyone uses daily. After a year, what happens to how people treat it on a real attack?
blocks.reveal: They click through by reflex. A warning that is usually wrong teaches people that proceeding is normal. Herley's 2009 paper made the extreme form of this point, claiming that "fully 100% of certificate error warnings appear to be false positives". Every unnecessary warning spends the attention a real one will need. Fix the noisy cause (renew internal certificates, use an internal certificate authority) instead of training people to ignore the screen.

blocks.md: **The best warning is no decision at all.** When the right answer never depends on the user's judgement, remove the choice. **HSTS** (HTTP Strict Transport Security, [RFC 6797](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6797)) lets a site tell browsers to reach it only over HTTPS. For a site that has sent this header, RFC 6797 says certificate errors must be handled with "no user recourse": the user "should not be presented with a dialog giving her the option to proceed". The click-through rate becomes zero by construction.

blocks.code:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains

# max-age: remember this rule for 31,536,000 seconds (one year)
# includeSubDomains: apply it to every subdomain too
# Effect (RFC 6797, 8.4 and 12.1): on any TLS error for this host the
# browser ends the connection and offers no 'proceed anyway' link.
blocks.caption: An HSTS response header and what it does. The site removes the dangerous decision instead of asking users to make it well.

blocks.md: **Defender view.** Inventory the security prompts your own systems show (certificate errors, "enable content" bars, MFA approvals, "external sender" banners). For each, ask: how often is it a false alarm, could the system decide instead, and if a person must decide, is the safe choice the visually obvious one? Measure adherence where you can; a prompt with 70% clickthrough is not a control.
Warnings work when they are rare, specific and opinionated, and fail when they are frequent and neutral. Where the safe answer is always the same, block instead of warning.

blocks.question: Chrome's 2013 SSL warning had 70.2% clickthrough while its malware warning had 23.2%. What does Akhawe and Felt's comparison mostly show?
options: Chrome users are more reckless than Firefox users
The presentation and context of a warning strongly change behaviour
SSL errors are always harmless
Malware warnings are shown less often
blocks.explain: Chrome users heeded most malware warnings, and Firefox users heeded most SSL warnings. The large difference for one warning type in one browser points at that warning's design and context, not at the users.

blocks.question: Which change would most reliably stop users proceeding to an attacker's site on a bank's domain with a forged certificate?
options: A longer warning text that explains certificates
A warning with a red background
The bank sends HSTS, so the browser refuses the connection with no option to proceed
Training customers to read certificate details
blocks.explain: HSTS removes the decision: for a known HSTS host the browser must terminate on any certificate error. Explanations and colours help adherence but still leave a click-through path.

lessons.title: Password and MFA friction: rules that backfire and rules that work

blocks.md:
Tiny example. A site demands a capital letter, a digit and a symbol. The user who wanted "password" types "Password1!" and the rule is satisfied. NIST's guidance uses exactly this example: research shows users respond "in very predictable ways" to composition rules, so "password" becomes "Password1" and then "Password1!". The rule cost effort and bought almost no security, because attackers guess those predictable patterns first.

**NIST SP 800-63B** is the US National Institute of Standards and Technology's guideline on authentication (SP means Special Publication). Its fourth revision (800-63B-4, July 2025) turned two decades of usable-security findings into rules.

What 800-63B-4 requires of a verifier (the system that checks a password):

- Passwords used alone (single-factor) must be **at least 15 characters**; passwords used only as part of MFA may be **as short as 8**.
- It **SHALL NOT** impose other composition rules (mixtures of character types).
- It **SHALL NOT** require periodic changes, but SHALL force a change if there is evidence of compromise.
- New passwords are compared against a **blocklist** of common, expected or compromised values, and the reason for a rejection is shown.
- It SHALL allow password managers and autofill, and SHOULD allow at least 64 characters, accept spaces and all printing characters, and permit paste.
- No password hints and no **knowledge-based authentication** (KBA: "What was your first pet's name?" questions).

Notice the direction: fewer rules for the user, more checking by the system.

blocks.code:
import unicodedata

# Tiny stand-in; a real blocklist holds known-breached and common passwords.
BLOCKLIST = {"password", "password1", "password1!", "qwerty123456789",
             "correcthorsebatterystaple"}

def check(pw, single_factor=True):
    pw = unicodedata.normalize("NFC", pw)    # one code point = one character
    minimum = 15 if single_factor else 8
    if len(pw) < minimum:
        return f"reject: shorter than {minimum}"
    if len(pw) > 64:
        return "reject: longer than our 64-character maximum"
    if pw.lower() in BLOCKLIST:
        return "reject: on the blocklist (choose something less common)"
    return "accept"          # no rules about digits, symbols or case

for pw, sf in [("Password1!", True), ("Password1!", False),
               ("correcthorsebatterystaple", True),
               ("tram lamp under the ninth bridge", True)]:
    print(f"{pw!r:36} single-factor={sf!s:5} {check(pw, sf)}")

# Output:
# 'Password1!'                         single-factor=True  reject: shorter than 15
# 'Password1!'                         single-factor=False reject: on the blocklist (choose something less common)
# 'correcthorsebatterystaple'          single-factor=True  reject: on the blocklist (choose something less common)
# 'tram lamp under the ninth bridge'   single-factor=True  accept
blocks.caption: A verifier following 800-63B-4: length and a blocklist, no composition rules. A real blocklist holds known-breached and common passwords, not five entries.

blocks.md:
**MFA friction.** **Multi-factor authentication** asks for something more than a password. The cheapest form for users is a **push notification**: the phone shows "Approve sign-in?" and one tap answers. That convenience is the weakness. An attacker who already has the password can trigger prompt after prompt; CISA (the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) calls this **MFA fatigue** or "push bombing": bombarding a user with prompts "until the user either approves the request by accident or out of annoyance".

**Case: Uber, September 2022.** [Uber's own update](https://www.uber.com/us/en/newsroom/security-update/) said an external contractor's corporate password was likely bought on the dark web; the attacker "repeatedly tried to log in", the contractor received a two-factor approval request each time, and "Eventually, however, the contractor accepted one".

blocks.title: Push bombing, then the number-matching fix

scenes.caption: The attacker has a stolen password and signs in. The identity provider (IdP, the service that checks logins) sends a push prompt to the real user's phone.
The user did not start a login and denies it. The attacker simply tries again, and again. Each prompt looks identical to a real one.
Tired, distracted or told by a fake IT message to accept, the user taps Approve once. The attacker is in. One tap of consent was all the factor required.
Number matching: the login screen shows a number and the phone asks the user to type it. Only the person looking at the real login screen knows it, so a stray prompt cannot be approved by a tap.

blocks.md:
[CISA recommends](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/publications/fact-sheet-implement-number-matching-in-mfa-applications-508c.pdf) **phishing-resistant MFA** (security keys and passkeys, which the phishing course showed are bound to the real site) and, where that is not yet possible, **number matching** as "one of the best interim" mitigations.

**Friction pushes attackers to recovery.** Stronger login factors move the weakest point to account recovery: what happens when someone loses their phone. 800-63B-4 says an account recovery event "always causes one or more notifications to be sent to the subscriber", and that recovery is expected to be less convenient than authentication. Recovery is usually run by people at a help desk, which is why the next lessons focus there.

Misconception: "more password rules means more security". Composition rules and forced changes make people choose predictable variants and write them down. Length, a blocklist, rate limiting, and MFA that is bound to the site do the real work.

blocks.question: Under NIST SP 800-63B-4, which policy is allowed for a password used as a single factor?
options: Minimum 15 characters, checked against a blocklist, no composition rules
Minimum 8 characters, must contain a digit and a symbol
Must be changed every 90 days
Must have a hint so users can recover it
blocks.explain: Single-factor passwords need at least 15 characters. Composition rules, periodic changes and hints are all prohibited by SHALL NOT statements in the guideline.

blocks.question: A company's push-based MFA is being bombed with prompts. As an interim step before phishing-resistant MFA, which change does CISA recommend?
options: Lock the account after one denied prompt
Send prompts by SMS instead
Ask users to approve only during business hours
Enable number matching so approving requires typing the number shown on the real login screen
blocks.explain: Number matching ties approval to the login screen the real user is looking at, so blind or accidental approvals stop working. SMS is weaker, and time-of-day rules do not stop a determined attacker.

lessons.title: Anatomy of a pretext: how manipulation is built and broken

blocks.md:
Picture a phone call to the payroll team from someone claiming to work in IT, who says an urgent change is due tonight and asks the employee to read out a one-time code from their phone. Nothing in it is technical. Its power comes from a believable story, a role with authority, a deadline and a small, specific request, and it fails against one rule: codes are never read out to anyone.

That story is a **pretext**: an invented scenario in which the attacker plays a role so that the target releases information or takes an action. CAPEC (Common Attack Pattern Enumeration and Classification, MITRE's public catalogue of attack patterns) lists pretexting as [pattern 407](https://capec.mitre.org/data/definitions/407.html) and notes it is "more than just creating a lie": sometimes a whole new identity is built to sustain it.

Defenders find it useful to break a social engineering attack into stages, because each stage leaves traces and each can be interrupted:

1. **Research.** Names, roles, reporting lines, internal jargon and processes, from social media, job adverts and earlier calls. CISA's Scattered Spider advisory (AA23-320A) says the group's first calls are "designed to first learn what steps are needed to conduct password resets". Gathering organisational facts this way is what NIST calls **social mining**.
2. **Contact and rapport.** A channel (phone, SMS, chat, in person) and a reason to talk. **Elicitation** is drawing out information through conversation without asking for it directly.
3. **The ask.** One action that serves the attacker: read out a code, reset a password, open a door, install a remote support tool, pay an invoice.
4. **Exit.** Leaving without alarm, often with a reason to keep quiet ("this is confidential").

The persuasion levers you met in the phishing course (authority, urgency, liking) operate inside stages 2 and 3.

blocks.title: The stages of a pretext, and where each one can be broken

scenes.caption: Four stages. Most organisations defend only the third one, the moment a person decides, which is where the attacker has the most control.
Research: reduce what you publish about internal processes and staff, and treat 'how do resets work here?' calls as reportable events.
Contact: the caller controls caller ID, chat display names and email display names. A control that never trusts the inbound channel removes their advantage.
The ask: a process rule (call back on a number from the directory; no codes are ever read aloud) decides, so the person does not have to out-argue a skilled caller.
Exit: a culture where reporting is quick and thanked turns 'something felt odd' into an early warning for everyone else the attacker is calling.

blocks.md:
**How the catalogues name it.** NIST SP 800-53 (the US federal catalogue of security controls) lists the forms that awareness training should cover: "phishing, pretexting, impersonation, baiting, quid pro quo, thread-jacking, social media exploitation, and tailgating". **Baiting** leaves a lure, such as a USB stick, for someone to pick up; **quid pro quo** (Latin, "something for something") offers a favour such as free IT help in return for an action; **thread-jacking** replies inside a real email thread from a compromised account.

MITRE ATT&CK (the public catalogue of attacker techniques) added a technique called **Social Engineering** (T1684) in 2026, and moved its impersonation technique there as T1684.001 (it was T1656). Phone-based phishing is Spearphishing Voice, T1566.004.

blocks.code:
# The directory is the only source of numbers. Anything the caller
# offers (a number, a name, a ticket ID) is a claim, not a proof.
DIRECTORY = {"dana.ruiz": "ext 2210", "it.servicedesk": "ext 1000"}

def handle(claimed_identity, request, offered_number=None):
    if claimed_identity not in DIRECTORY:
        return "no such person: end the call, report it"
    number = DIRECTORY[claimed_identity]
    note = " (ignore the number the caller gave)" if offered_number else ""
    return f"hang up, call {number}{note}, then decide on: {request}"

print(handle("dana.ruiz", "read me the code on your phone"))
print(handle("it.servicedesk", "install this remote support tool",
             offered_number="+1 555 0100"))
print(handle("it-helpdesk-team", "reset your password on my page"))

# Output:
# hang up, call ext 2210, then decide on: read me the code on your phone
# hang up, call ext 1000 (ignore the number the caller gave), then decide on: install this remote support tool
# no such person: end the call, report it
blocks.caption: The callback rule as code. The person never has to judge whether the voice is genuine; the directory is the only source of numbers.

blocks.md: **Defender view.** Prevention: write process rules that make the decisive step independent of the conversation (callbacks to directory numbers, codes never read aloud, no software installed at a caller's request) and let staff refuse without penalty. Detection: reports of odd calls, especially several on the same day; chat messages from external accounts with names like "helpdesk" (Mandiant advises monitoring for these in collaboration tools such as Microsoft Teams); lookalike domains containing your name plus "helpdesk" or "sso". Response: warn the teams being called, because pretext campaigns usually work down a list.
Do not ask people to detect lies in real time. Give them a rule that does not depend on the caller being honest, and make following the rule faster than arguing.

blocks.question: A caller claiming to be from IT gives a callback number 'in case we get cut off'. What should the employee do to verify the caller?
options: Call the number given, since that proves the caller answers it
Ask the caller three questions only real IT staff would know
Look up the service desk in the company directory and call that number instead
Check that caller ID shows the company's name
blocks.explain: A number supplied by the caller leads back to the caller. Caller ID and display names are set by the caller too. Only a number from a source the caller does not control, such as the directory, verifies anything.

blocks.question: In CISA's description of Scattered Spider, what was the purpose of the group's first calls to a help desk?
options: To learn what steps are needed for a password reset, so later calls could follow them convincingly
To install ransomware directly
To test whether phones were monitored
To ask for a job
blocks.explain: AA23-320A says the early attempts were designed to learn the reset steps, then later calls gathered details about a target employee. Research calls are a detection opportunity if staff report them.

blocks.question: An attacker offers employees free 'priority IT support' if they install a remote access tool. Which form in NIST's list is this?
options: Thread-jacking
Quid pro quo
Tailgating
Baiting
blocks.explain: Quid pro quo offers a service or favour in return for an action. Baiting leaves an object as a lure; thread-jacking hijacks an existing email conversation; tailgating is physical.

lessons.title: Voice clones and deepfake meetings: when seeing is not believing

blocks.md:
For years the advice for a suspicious email was "pick up the phone" or "get on a video call": hearing and seeing a colleague felt like proof. Generative AI weakened that proof. A **deepfake** is synthetic media; FinCEN (the US Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network) defines deepfakes as content made with artificial intelligence or machine learning "to create realistic but inauthentic videos, pictures, audio, and text". A **voice clone** is synthetic speech in a particular person's voice, built from recordings of them.

The defence lesson is the same as for any pretext, but sharper: the more convincing the channel, the less a person's judgement of it should decide anything.

**Case: Arup, Hong Kong, January 2024.** In February 2024 Hong Kong police [described a case](https://edition.cnn.com/2024/02/04/asia/deepfake-cfo-scam-hong-kong-intl-hnk) without naming the company. A finance worker received a message that claimed to come from the firm's UK-based chief financial officer (CFO) about a secret transaction. The worker first suspected a phishing email. Then came a multi-person video conference in which, as senior superintendent Baron Chan Shun-ching told the public broadcaster RTHK, "it turns out that everyone [he saw] was fake". Believing the others on the call were real, the worker sent a total of HKD 200 million (about USD 25.6 million) in 15 transactions, according to RTHK citing police. The fraud was discovered only when the worker later checked with the head office.

In May 2024 Arup, the London-based design and engineering firm, confirmed to CNN that it was the company, that it had notified Hong Kong police in January, and that "fake voices and images were used".

blocks.title: Arup 2024: where the doubt was overcome (simplified order of events)

scenes.caption: A message arrives in the CFO's name asking for a secret transaction. The worker's instinct is right: it looks like phishing.
The attackers answer the doubt with a richer channel: a video meeting with the CFO and colleagues, all generated. The worker's check was real; the evidence it produced was fake.
Fifteen transfers, HKD 200 million in all. Nothing reported shows a check through a channel the requester did not control before the money moved.
Discovery comes from an out-of-band check with head office, the step that would have stopped the loss if it had come before the first transfer.

blocks.prompt: The Arup worker did the 'right' thing by doubting the email and then seeing the CFO on video. What should the payment process have required instead of the worker's judgement?
blocks.reveal: A confirmation that does not travel through any channel the requester set up. For example: a callback to the CFO on a number from the company directory, plus a second approver for new beneficiaries above a threshold. A video call arranged by the requester is part of the requester's channel, however real it looks. The rule should make **how convincing the request seems** irrelevant to whether money moves.

blocks.code:
# Numbers come from HR records, never from the request itself.
DIRECTORY = {"cfo": "ext 4471"}

def release(p):
    why = []
    if p["new_beneficiary"] and not p["callback_to"]:
        why.append("new beneficiary not confirmed by callback")
    if p["callback_to"] and p["callback_to"] != DIRECTORY[p["requester"]]:
        why.append("callback used a number supplied by the requester")
    if p["amount"] >= 100_000 and len(p["approvers"]) < 2:
        why.append("needs a second approver")
    return why or ["release"]

# How convincing the request looked is deliberately not an input.
p = {"requester": "cfo", "amount": 1_700_000, "new_beneficiary": True,
     "callback_to": None, "approvers": ["clerk"]}
print(release(p))
p["callback_to"] = "number from the meeting chat"
print(release(p))
p.update(callback_to=DIRECTORY["cfo"], approvers=["clerk", "controller"])
print(release(p))

# Output:
# ['new beneficiary not confirmed by callback', 'needs a second approver']
# ['callback used a number supplied by the requester', 'needs a second approver']
# ['release']
blocks.caption: A payment release rule. Nothing about the video call, the voice or the urgency is an input; only callbacks to directory numbers and a second approver count.

blocks.md: **Voice impersonation of officials.** In May 2025 the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) warned that since April 2025 malicious actors had impersonated senior US officials with text messages and "AI-generated voice messages" to build rapport and then move targets to another platform. Its advice is process, not perception: before responding, "independently identify a phone number for the person and call to verify their authenticity", and if someone you know contacts you on a new platform or number, verify it "through a previously confirmed platform or trusted source". It lists visual and audio artefacts to look for, but also concedes that cloned voices "can sound nearly identical" and AI content "is often difficult to identify".

[FinCEN's November 2024 alert](https://www.fincen.gov/system/files/shared/FinCEN-Alert-DeepFakes-Alert508FINAL.pdf) adds a second target: criminals using altered or synthetic identity documents and images "to circumvent identity verification and authentication methods". That includes the video checks that help desks are now told to use (lesson 8), so a video check should never be the only proof.

Misconception: "train people to spot deepfakes". Spotting artefacts is a losing race as tools improve, and the IC3 itself says AI content is often hard to identify. Teach the artefacts as a reason to pause, but make the decision depend on an independent channel.

**Defender view.** Prevention: callbacks to directory numbers for any payment, credential or access change; two-person approval for new payees; agreed internal words or ticket references that never appear in public channels, for the highest-value requests; and executives saying in advance "I will never ask you to bypass this". Detection: payment-change requests that arrive with secrecy and urgency, new beneficiary accounts, and requests that move the conversation to a new platform. Response: contact your bank at once to try to recall the transfers, preserve the meeting invitation, recordings and chat logs, and report to police.

blocks.question: A manager receives a voice message that sounds exactly like the CEO asking for an urgent transfer, followed by a text from a new number. Which response matches the IC3's guidance?
options: Reply to the text asking a personal question only the CEO would know
Listen for audio glitches; if none, proceed
Forward the voice message to a deepfake detection website and proceed if it says genuine
Call the CEO on a number already on record and confirm before doing anything
blocks.explain: The IC3 advises independently finding the person's number and calling to verify, and verifying new contact details through a previously confirmed channel. Personal questions can be researched, and detection is unreliable.

blocks.question: Why is a video call that the requester arranges weak evidence of identity, even if the faces look right?
options: Because the requester controls that channel, so its content can be fabricated end to end
Because video calls are always encrypted
Because faces cannot be seen clearly on video
Because video calls are not recorded
blocks.explain: In the Arup case every participant except the victim was generated. Evidence produced inside a channel the attacker set up proves nothing about identity; only an independent channel does.

lessons.title: The help desk as an attack surface: MGM, Okta's warning and Clorox

blocks.md:
An IT **help desk** (also called a service desk) exists to get locked-out people working again, quickly and politely. That is exactly what an attacker needs. A help desk can reset passwords, re-register MFA devices and unlock accounts, which means it can hand over any account if it can be persuaded the caller is the owner. As login factors got stronger (lesson 4), attackers moved to the people who are allowed to replace them.

CISA and the FBI's advisory **AA23-320A** on Scattered Spider (first published November 2023, updated 29 July 2025) describes the pattern in its own words. The group "posed as employees to convince IT and/or helpdesk staff to provide sensitive information, reset the employee's password, and transfer the employee's MFA to a device they control". It also works in reverse: "Impersonating helpdesk personnel", the group directs employees "to run commercial remote access tools". The 2020 Twitter calls from the phishing course were this second direction: callers posing as IT talked staff into giving up credentials.

blocks.title: The help-desk takeover pattern (from AA23-320A and Okta's report)

scenes.caption: Reconnaissance calls: the attacker asks how resets work and what the agent will ask for. Nothing is reset, so nothing is logged as an incident.
The real call: the attacker poses as a specific employee, often a privileged one, armed with personal details from research or data for sale.
The agent resets the password and registers the attacker's device as the MFA factor. To the identity provider this is an authorised change.
The attacker signs in with the new factor, from a new device and often through an anonymising proxy. Every check passes.
With an admin account (Okta's cases targeted Super Administrators), the attacker changes the identity system itself, then reaches other applications as other users.

blocks.md: **Okta's warning, 31 August 2023.** Okta, a major identity provider, reported that "multiple US-based Okta customers" had seen "a consistent pattern of social engineering attacks against their IT service desk personnel", in which callers tried to get the agent "to reset all Multi-factor Authentication (MFA) factors enrolled by highly privileged users". The callers appeared either to have the privileged users' passwords already or to be able to manipulate delegated authentication (Okta handing password checks to the company's own Active Directory, Microsoft's directory of staff accounts). With the compromised Super Administrator accounts, they set up a second identity provider they controlled in an **inbound federation** relationship (one identity system trusting logins from another), which let them sign in to applications as other users.

**MGM Resorts, September 2023.** The Financial Times, republished by Ars Technica, reported that Scattered Spider was the likely culprit in the attack that shut down large parts of MGM's network on the Las Vegas Strip, and that the group uses fraudulent phone calls to employees and help desks. MGM did not comment to the reporters, so the entry method remains reported, not confirmed. In an October 2023 filing to the US SEC (Securities and Exchange Commission), [MGM estimated](https://lasvegassun.com/news/2023/oct/05/mgm-estimates-losses-at-100-million-from-september/) a negative impact of about USD 100 million, plus less than USD 10 million in one-time expenses.

**Clorox and Cognizant (lawsuit filed July 2025).** These are **allegations**; Cognizant disputes them. Clorox, the US consumer goods maker, sued its former service-desk provider Cognizant for USD 380 million over the August 2023 attack that disrupted its operations; Clorox says it spent USD 49 million on remediation ([The Record](https://therecord.media/clorox-cyberattack-lawsuit-cognizant-it-contractor)).

Per the complaint, as reported by The Register, Clorox's procedure told agents to guide callers to its self-service reset tool (MyID) or, if that was unavailable, to verify the caller by manager name and MyID username, and then send confirmation emails to the employee and the manager. The complaint alleges an agent reset the password "without any further questioning or identity verification", reset the Microsoft MFA credentials "multiple times without any identity verification at all", and was asked to change the SMS MFA phone number. Cognizant's response: Clorox "hired Cognizant for a narrow scope of help desk services which Cognizant reasonably performed".

Two lessons sit in that dispute, whichever side is right. First, a written procedure is a control only if it is followed under pressure, so it must be checked against what agents actually log. Second, even the written procedure leaned on facts (a manager's name, a username) that an attacker can often research. The script below audits ticket logs against the procedure; lesson 8 designs stronger proofs.

blocks.caption: Auditing help-desk tickets against the written procedure: sensitive actions need a prior identity check, and the user and manager must be notified. HD-102 is shaped like the allegations, not copied from any real log.

blocks.md: The help desk is an authentication system made of people. It needs the same design care as a login page: what proof it accepts, what it logs, who is notified, and how it is tested. The Bank of England's [2025 CBEST thematic](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/financial-stability/operational-resilience-of-the-financial-sector/2025-cbest-thematic) (lessons from regulated red team tests of UK financial firms) lists helpdesks with "limited or no authentication of users" as a finding.

blocks.question: Okta's 2023 report described callers asking help desks to reset all MFA factors for Super Administrators. Why target those accounts specifically?
options: They have weaker passwords
Admin accounts can change the identity system itself, opening every other account and application
Help desks cannot see who is an administrator
Super Administrators never use MFA
blocks.explain: Control of the identity provider's admin role let the attackers add their own identity provider and sign in as other users. One reset on the right account is worth hundreds on ordinary ones.

blocks.question: A help desk procedure requires 'manager name and username' before a reset. What is its main weakness?
options: It takes too long
It requires a manager to be online
Both facts are often discoverable from public profiles, org charts or earlier calls, so they do not prove identity
Usernames are secret by design
blocks.explain: Mandiant's hardening guide warns against relying on publicly available personal data because the group 'often possesses this information'. Proof must be something the attacker cannot research or buy.

lessons.title: Designing help-desk verification that holds under pressure

blocks.md:
Lesson 7 showed what fails: identity checks based on facts an attacker can look up. This lesson builds the replacement. The goal: an agent can say yes quickly to a real employee and no confidently to an impostor, without having to judge anyone's voice or story.

Start from a ranking of proofs by how hard they are for an attacker to get:

- **Weak (knowable):** name, employee ID, date of birth, manager's name, last four digits of a national ID number, a callback number the caller supplies. NIST 800-63B-4 already bans knowledge-based questions for passwords; Mandiant's guidance says to avoid "publicly available personal data for verification (e.g., DOB, last 4 SSN)".
- **Out-of-band:** a callback to a number already on file, or approval by the manager inside the ticket system. These go through channels the caller does not control.
- **Strong:** signing in with an existing factor (a passkey), an on-camera or in-person check against the photo ID on file.

**What the guidance asks for.** Mandiant's 2025 hardening guide for this threat (it tracks Scattered Spider as UNC3944) says to "positively identify employees before modifying / providing security information (including initial enrollment)", at minimum for privileged accounts, with methods such as "On-Camera / In-Person verification", "ID Verification" and challenge and response questions. It adds: require strong authentication "PRIOR to changing authentication methods", use "Out-of-band verification for high-risk changes", and consider temporarily disabling self-service MFA resets "during elevated threat periods".

Okta's list adds: "Strengthen help desk identity verification processes using visual verification", turn on new-device and suspicious-activity notifications to users, and "Constrain custom help desk roles" so agents cannot reset the most privileged administrators at all.

Because lesson 6 showed that video can be faked, the design below never lets a video check alone unlock a privileged account.

blocks.title: A verification policy for MFA reset calls

scenes.caption: Three sets of proofs. Facts an attacker can research or buy are listed only so the policy can name them when it refuses.
Call 1: name, employee ID and date of birth. None is strong or out-of-band, so the agent declines and offers the real paths.
scenes.output:
user  name + employee_id + date_of_birth
      deny: 3 facts, all of them easy to look up or buy

scenes.caption: Call 2: the agent hangs up and calls the number on file; the real employee answers. Good enough for an ordinary account.
scenes.output:
user  callback_to_number_on_file
      allow: then notify user on old factor and alert the SOC

scenes.caption: Call 3: an administrator on camera matches the ID photo on file. One strong proof is not enough for a privileged account, because video can be faked.
scenes.output:
admin video_match_to_id_on_file
      deny: privileged account needs strong AND out-of-band

scenes.caption: Call 4: the video match plus the manager approving inside the ticket system. Two independent proofs, so the reset goes ahead, followed by notifications.
scenes.output:
admin video_match_to_id_on_file + manager_approves_in_ticket
      allow: then notify user on old factor and alert the SOC

blocks.md:
Line 11 is the cheapest path of all: a person who can still sign in with a passkey can reset their own password without any agent. The more people can recover through self-service with a strong factor, the fewer calls the help desk must judge.

**After the reset.** Every change should trigger notifications to the old factor and the user's manager (NIST says account recovery "always causes one or more notifications"), and an alert to the **SOC** (security operations centre, the team that watches for and responds to attacks). A reset followed within minutes by a sign-in from a new device and an unusual location is the signal to investigate; the course "Security operations: alert triage and investigation" builds that detection.

**The people side.** A procedure only holds if agents are allowed to use it. Concretely:

- Give agents a short, polite refusal they can say without escalating: "I can't change that over the phone; here are the two ways I can help."
- Measure agents on correct verifications, not only on speed; a ticket closed fast by an impostor is a failure.
- Make "I think this caller is not who they say" a one-click flag that goes to the SOC, and thank agents who use it.
- Apply the same rules to outsourced help desks by contract, and audit their tickets (lesson 7).
- Rehearse: run authorised test calls against the procedure (lesson 14) and fix what breaks.

Misconception: "on-camera verification solves help-desk fraud". It raises the bar, but synthetic video and stolen ID images are already used against identity checks (FinCEN, 2024). Pair it with an out-of-band confirmation for anything privileged, and keep the most powerful admin accounts out of help-desk reach entirely.

blocks.question: Under the policy above, an ordinary employee calls to reset MFA and offers only their employee ID and date of birth. What should the agent do?
options: Decline the reset and offer a callback to the number on file or an in-person check
Reset it, since two facts were given
Reset it but only for 24 hours
Ask for their manager's name as a third fact
blocks.explain: All three facts are researchable; adding a third knowable fact changes nothing. The agent should move the caller onto a proof the attacker cannot supply, such as a callback to the number on file.

blocks.question: Why does the policy require two independent proofs for privileged accounts even after a successful video check?
options: Video calls are slow
Privileged users are more often impostors
A single proof can be faked or stolen, and a privileged account can change the identity system itself
Managers always approve requests
blocks.explain: The impact of a wrong decision is highest for admins (Okta's cases), and synthetic video weakens video checks. Two proofs through different channels mean an attacker must defeat both.

blocks.question: Which change most reduces the number of risky judgement calls the help desk has to make at all?
options: Longer calls with more personal questions
Self-service recovery that requires an existing strong factor, such as a passkey
Allowing resets by email
Publishing the help desk's verification questions
blocks.explain: If most people can recover by proving a factor they still hold, only the rare cases with no factor left reach an agent, and those can get the slow, strong checks.

lessons.title: SIM swaps, bribed insiders and people you do not employ

blocks.md:
Your phone number is often a key: SMS codes, password-reset texts and "call me to verify" all go to it. But the number belongs to the mobile carrier, and the carrier has its own help desks and retail stores. Persuade them, and the number moves.

The US FCC (Federal Communications Commission) defines the two moves in its [fact sheet](https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DOC-397990A1.pdf) on the rules. **SIM swapping**: a bad actor "convinces a victim's wireless provider to transfer the victim's mobile service and number" to a device the attacker holds (a **SIM**, subscriber identity module, is the chip or eSIM profile that ties a phone to a number). **Port-out fraud**: the attacker, posing as the victim, opens an account with another provider and has the number "ported out" to it. Either way, every SMS code now goes to the attacker, "without ever gaining physical control of a consumer's phone".

blocks.title: One phone number, many doors: how a SIM swap chains into accounts

nodes.label:
Services: no SMS as
a factor or for reset

scenes.caption: The attacker never touches the victim's phone. The target is the carrier's process for moving a number.
Persuaded, bribed or tricked carrier staff move the number to the attacker's SIM. The victim's phone silently loses service.
Every service that trusts SMS for login codes or password resets now sends them to the attacker: email, bank, work single sign-on (SSO, one login that opens many work apps).
Defences on both sides: carriers must authenticate before SIM changes and notify customers; your services stop trusting SMS, so the number is no longer a key.

blocks.md: **The FCC's rules.** In an order published in the Federal Register on 8 December 2023, the FCC required wireless providers to "adopt secure methods of authenticating a customer before redirecting a customer's phone number to a new device or provider" and to "immediately notify customers whenever a SIM change or port-out request is made". The order's fact sheet adds: processes for failed authentication attempts, employee training on SIM swap fraud, keeping customer-facing staff from seeing account data until the customer is authenticated, and letting customers **lock** their accounts against SIM changes and ports.

**The insider angle: Lapsus$.** The US Cyber Safety Review Board (CSRB, a body that reviews major incidents) studied Lapsus$ and related groups, which hit large companies in 2021 and 2022, sometimes with teenage members. It found that some "used monetary incentives to recruit employees and contractors of targeted organizations", who handed over credentials, approved MFA requests or acted directly. For access at telecommunications providers, the group offered "as much as" USD 20,000 per week to conduct SIM swaps. It also co-opted employees in carrier retail stores, which the Board called hard to counter because such jobs are "typically lower pay with low-vetted personnel".

The CSRB's conclusion on MFA: one-time codes and pushes delivered "using SMS and voice calls (and even email) are vulnerable to social engineering and SIM swap attacks". If your organisation still uses SMS as a factor or for account recovery, the security of every account rests partly on the weakest store clerk at every carrier your staff use.

**Case: the Tesla employee who said no (2020).** A Russian national, Egor Kriuchkov, tried to recruit an employee at Tesla's Nevada battery plant to install malware on the company network so that data could be stolen for ransom. The employee reported the approach to company officials, Tesla brought in the FBI, and Kriuchkov was arrested in August 2020. At sentencing in May 2021 ([AP via Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2021/5/24/us-to-deport-russian-man-who-tried-to-hack-tesla)) the judge put the offer at USD 500,000; Kriuchkov had pleaded guilty to conspiracy to damage a protected computer; the 10-month sentence amounted to time served, then deportation. Federal authorities credited the employee with reporting the overtures.

blocks.prompt: A bribe to install malware is one of the hardest attacks to stop technically: the insider has legitimate access. What made the Tesla attempt fail?
blocks.reveal: A person reported it. The approach happened outside work systems, so no log or filter would have seen it. What worked was an employee who knew that reporting an approach was expected and safe, and a company that took the report to law enforcement quickly. Insider recruitment is ultimately defended by the same reporting culture as phishing (lesson 15), plus least privilege so that one recruited person cannot do everything.

blocks.md: **Defender view.** Prevention: remove SMS and voice from MFA and recovery for staff, starting with administrators; ask staff to enable carrier account locks or port-out PINs on work numbers; give every role only the access it needs, so a recruited insider's reach is limited. Detection: an employee's phone suddenly losing service is a SIM-swap symptom worth a call to the help desk; a sign-in using SMS shortly after a number change; staff reports of recruitment approaches, including on social media. Response: treat a confirmed SIM swap as an account compromise of everything tied to that number.

People outside your organisation (carrier staff, outsourced agents, contractors) can be the weak link for your accounts. Design so that no single outside person's mistake or bribe hands over a login, and make reporting approaches normal inside.

blocks.question: Which change removes most of the value of a SIM swap against your employees' work accounts?
options: Asking carriers to train their staff
Requiring phishing-resistant MFA and recovery that never relies on SMS or voice
Telling employees to keep their phones charged
Using longer passwords
blocks.explain: If codes and resets never go to the phone number, moving the number gains the attacker nothing at work. Carrier rules help, but you cannot control every carrier's staff.

blocks.question: The CSRB found Lapsus$ paid insiders at telecom providers. Why is that hard to counter with technical controls alone?
options: The insider uses legitimate access, so the action looks like normal work
Insiders always use encrypted messages
Telecom systems have no logs
Bribes are legal in some countries
blocks.explain: An insider approving an MFA request or doing a SIM swap is using tools they are allowed to use. Least privilege, strong customer authentication before sensitive actions, and reporting channels matter more than filters.

lessons.title: Physical security in layers: zones, CPTED and access rules

blocks.md:
Everything so far assumed the attacker is outside. Now suppose they walk in. A person inside a building can plug a device into a network port, take a laptop, read a whiteboard, photograph papers, or sit at an unlocked screen. Physical access defeats many logical controls, so physical security is part of information security: NIST SP 800-53 has a whole family of controls for it (PE, Physical and Environmental Protection).

NIST's basic physical access control (PE-3) asks an organisation to: verify individual access authorisations before granting access; control entry and exit with access control systems or guards; keep physical access audit logs; escort visitors; secure keys, combinations and other access devices; inventory them; and change combinations and keys when they are lost or when people who hold them leave.

**Zones.** Rather than one front door guarding everything, facilities are divided into nested areas, each requiring more proof than the one outside it. NIST SP 800-116 (on using government smart cards for building access) uses three levels, mapped to the impact of what they protect:

- **Controlled** area: proof of affiliation (any employee or contractor), at least **1** authentication factor.
- **Limited** area: a role or group (a division's wing), at least **2** factors.
- **Exclusion** area: individual authorisation only, at least **3** factors.

A **factor** is something you have (a card), know (a PIN) or are (a fingerprint). Because areas are nested, a door may count factors already proven at outer doors, which NIST calls authentication "in context". The script checks a path through the zones.

blocks.code:
# NIST SP 800-116r1, Table 4-3: minimum authentication factors per area.
REQUIRED = {"controlled": 1, "limited": 2, "exclusion": 3}

# Each door checks some factors. Nested areas can count factors
# already proven at the doors on the way in ("authentication in context").
path = [("controlled", {"have"}),          # card with challenge-response
        ("limited",    {"are"}),           # fingerprint
        ("exclusion",  {"know", "have"})]  # PIN plus card again

proven = set()
for area, factors in path:
    proven |= factors
    ok = len(proven) >= REQUIRED[area]
    print(f"{area:10} door checks {sorted(factors)!s:18} "
          f"proven so far {sorted(proven)!s:26} need {REQUIRED[area]}: "
          f"{'ok' if ok else 'NOT ENOUGH'}")

print()
print("Same building, but the limited-area door accepts any badge tap:")
proven = set()
for area, factors in [("controlled", {"have"}), ("limited", {"have"}),
                      ("exclusion", {"know", "have"})]:
    proven |= factors
    print(f"{area:10} proven {sorted(proven)!s:18} need {REQUIRED[area]}: "
          f"{'ok' if len(proven) >= REQUIRED[area] else 'NOT ENOUGH'}")

controlled door checks ['have']           proven so far ['have']                   need 1: ok
limited    door checks ['are']            proven so far ['are', 'have']            need 2: ok
exclusion  door checks ['have', 'know']   proven so far ['are', 'have', 'know']    need 3: ok

Same building, but the limited-area door accepts any badge tap:
controlled proven ['have']           need 1: ok
limited    proven ['have']           need 2: NOT ENOUGH
exclusion  proven ['have', 'know']   need 3: NOT ENOUGH
blocks.caption: Output of the script above. Checking a route through nested areas against NIST SP 800-116r1's minimum factors. The second building looks secure door by door, but the limited-area door asks only for the same card again, so the limited and exclusion areas fall short.

blocks.title: Nested areas: each layer adds proof

scenes.caption: The public area (lobby, reception) needs no credential. Its job is to observe and route visitors.
Controlled area: any badge holder, one factor. Most office floors live here.
Limited area: a role-based wing such as finance or the lab, two factors in total.
Exclusion area: the server room or vault, named individuals only, three factors. An entry vestibule (lesson 12) stops a second person slipping in behind.
Logs from every checkpoint feed one place, so a badge seen where it should not be, or a door held open, becomes an alert (PE-6: monitor physical access and coordinate with incident response).

blocks.md:
**CPTED: design the space so misuse is visible.** **Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design** is the idea that the layout of a place can make crime harder and riskier. It is named after the 1971 book *Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design* by the criminologist C. Ray Jeffery, which shifted attention from the offender to the circumstances around a crime. Oscar Newman, an architect, published *Defensible Space* in 1972, drawing on work in St Louis and New York City; it stressed territoriality and surveillance.

Timothy Crowe and Diane Zahm's 1994 summary names three design approaches:

- **Natural access control**: doors, fences, paths and landscaping that steer people to intended entrances.
- **Natural surveillance**: windows, lighting and sightlines so that people can see and be seen.
- **Territorial behaviour**: clear signs of ownership and boundaries, so an intruder stands out.

In an office: one obvious entrance that reception can see, no hidden side doors propped open for smokers, glass walls into the server corridor, and good lighting at the loading dock.

Misconception: "physical security is the facilities team's job". Many intrusion paths end at a network port or an unlocked laptop. Security engineers should own the requirements (which zones protect which systems, what gets logged, how alerts reach the SOC) together with facilities.

blocks.question: A building has three nested areas, and every door, including the server room, accepts a badge tap alone. Against NIST SP 800-116's table, what is wrong?
options: Nothing, as long as the badges are encrypted
The limited and exclusion areas get only one factor instead of the two and three they need
There are too many doors
Badges should only be used at the front door
blocks.explain: Repeating the same factor at every door proves nothing new. The limited area needs two factors and the exclusion area three, for example badge plus PIN plus fingerprint.

blocks.question: A company removes the bushes outside its ground-floor windows and lights the car park. Which CPTED approach is that?
options: Territorial behaviour
Natural access control
Natural surveillance
Target hardening with locks
blocks.explain: Clearing sightlines and adding light lets people see and be seen, which is natural surveillance. Access control steers movement; territorial behaviour marks ownership.

lessons.title: What a lock really does: pin tumblers, master keys and key control

blocks.md:
Security engineering borrowed its vocabulary from locksmiths: keys, locks, intruders. Matt Blaze, a computer security researcher then at AT&T Labs, turned the comparison around in a 2003 paper in *IEEE Security and Privacy* (a magazine of the IEEE, the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) and analysed mechanical locks the way one analyses a cryptographic protocol. His starting point: mechanical locks are the most common access control on doors, yet computer security people tend to accept claims about physical security with little scepticism.

This lesson explains, at the level of mechanism, what a common lock checks and what it cannot do, so that you can judge where locks fit among your controls. It does not teach how to open locks.

**The pin tumbler lock.** The most common keyed lock has a **plug** (the part that turns) inside a **shell** (the fixed body). Holes run through both, and each holds a **pin stack** pushed down by a spring. With no key, pins sit across the border between plug and shell and block rotation. That border is the **shear line**. A key's cuts lift each stack to a height; if every stack has a gap exactly at the shear line, the plug turns. A key's pattern of cut depths is called its **bitting**, written as digits (for example 11111 for five shallow cuts).

**Master keying.** Large buildings want one key per room plus keys that open many rooms. In the common scheme, each pin stack contains an extra cut, so two different depths per position align at the shear line: one for that room's own **change key**, one for the **master key**. Several levels are possible, up to a **top master key** that opens everything.

blocks.title: A master-keyed lock checks each pin separately (after Blaze, 2003)

scenes.caption: Each of the five pin stacks has two working depths: 1 (this room's change key) and 4 (the master key). The lock does not know which key is in it; it only checks each position.
The change key, bitting 11111: every stack has a gap at the shear line, so the plug turns.
The master key, bitting 44444, also aligns every stack. This is the design working as intended.
A key mixing the two, such as 14111, also turns the plug: in Blaze's words there is no 'communication' among pins. Each position answers on its own.

So the lock leaks information position by position, like an oracle in cryptography. Blaze showed that this lets the holder of one ordinary key and its lock work out the master key. The fix is organisational: limit what one key can unlock.

blocks.md:
**Rights amplification.** Blaze called this **rights amplification**: someone with legitimate access to one door (a tenant, a cleaner, a contractor) gains access to all of them. His [advisory](https://www.mattblaze.org/masterkey.html) says the attack "requires little skill, leaves behind no evidence", and that "virtually all master keyed mechanical lock systems are at least theoretically vulnerable". The paper also noted that master keying was already known to weaken locks: the master key "represents a very valuable target", and mastered locks are more prone to keys opening locks they should not.

The advisory says there is "no simple or completely effective countermeasure" short of dropping master keying; designs that resist the attack exist but "are not widely used commercially". Its practical advice is to split functions into separate master systems, so one key reaches less. The practical lesson for a security engineer is not about pins at all.

**A mechanical key is a bearer credential.** Whoever holds it is let in: it carries no identity, leaves no log, cannot be revoked remotely and can be copied. That is why NIST's PE-3 asks organisations to secure, inventory and **change keys and combinations when keys are lost or when holders leave**, and why rooms that matter are usually moved to electronic access control, where each person's credential can be revoked and every use is logged (lesson 12).

Also treat any lock as something that slows an intruder rather than stops one: pair it with a door alarm or sensor that detects forcing or a door left open, and with someone who responds.
